utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. If I could remind you, Colonel, of the affirmation that you took at the commencement of your evidence, which still applies. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. Yesterday you discussed the role of fire coordinators or fire executors as they provide orders and information to mortar operators, and you indicated that one of their roles is to issue commands or make adjustments, tell them to make certain adjustments, certain changes in their targeting. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The executor determines during the correction of the deviation and passes that on to the command -- to the unit at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, have you ever heard of a situation where mortar fire executors or coordinators failed to correct or adjust gross errors in targeting over a period of hours?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The firing executor, as soon as he spots an error, especially a gross error, will stop such firing, will provide the adequate correction, and then firing will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, I've got four brief questions for you for -- questions for clarification. First, if we could look at page 16 of your report in the English. It's page 16 in the English, and I'll give you the title. In the table at the top of the page, and that's the -- it's the expenditure norm table relating to neutralisation of "25 per cent on one hectare (observed target)." Under 8H and 9I in the explanation column you have the word "o/s" in both 8H and 9I. What does "o/s" mean? What does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are actually the means of firing, the firing means.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And below that, it says "The norms of expenditure apply to..." In the second one, it says, "Elements determined with full preparation of the battalion K or O," or is it KorO? What is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ammunition expenditure tables are drafted for certain firing conditions. First of all, for firing conditions where the firing elements are set by complete preparation of initial elements or base -- or based on corrective weapons of the battalion for the needs of the same battalion, the artillery battalion. One of the weapons is set, which makes the correction for the needs of that battalion or battery. So the correction data for the corrective weapons of the battalion is something that is later used by the whole battalion, all three units if we, for example, have three battalions which make up the -- three batteries which make up the battalion. So the corrective weapons of the battalion primarily for the mortar units is something that is not used. It's only used in artillery battalions. And some errors in the initial preparation of initial elements are determined by the corrective weapons to make sure that they are more or less the same, and that is why this is mentioned as a condition for which these tables are drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us what a corrective weapon is?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: A corrective weapon is one of the artillery weapons or one of the weapons in the artillery or the mortar unit or a battery or a platoon, also a division in the battalion, used to make corrections for the gauge or the target. The correction data for the benchmark are established to set the firing elements for a target within a certain area and a certain time period. Correction to the target means that at the end of the correction to the target, the corrective weapon, once that corrective weapon has finished its work, the group fire will start at the same target. So an average weapon would be used in a unit as a corrective weapon in a -- for -- or a central weapon, for example, in a mortar unit, out of six mortars, the third mortar would be used as a corrective weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I have another question on page 10 of the English. Just above the technical and tactical specification tables, and it's the sentence in the -- in the B/C/S, it would be just above -- there's a paragraph that says, "Mortars are light, heavy, and active --" "Mortar fire is light, heavy and active-reactive shells." Just above that, it says: "Mortars perform their tasks best in short fire strikes. Due to its construction, the number of shells that can be fired from the same position is limited." What do you mean by "the number of shells that can be fired from the same position is limited"?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the mortar's construction and because a mortar does not have an anti-recoil system, the whole pressure of firing is transferred from the weapon to the base and from the base to the surface of the earth. So the earth gets packed, the earth on which the base is placed. So after a certain amount of projectiles are fired, there is instability and there is a probability that the mortar might tip over, and that is why the rules provide that, depending on the hardness of the ground, to fire a certain number of projectiles from a certain position, a certain number of shells, and then the weapon is moved by five, six, or ten metres and firing continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P182, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you look at that chart here, there's columns 1, 2, 3 and 4. Column 5 is missing, column 10 is missing, 13 through 17 are missing, column 20 is missing. Why are some of these columns missing? Are those located on another page or is there a reason for that?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the columns are missing, then those elements are not necessary for that particular firing. Perhaps they would be in some other firing tables for Howitzers of 105 and 155. So those columns which are marked in the firing tables are those which are essential in order to actually execute the firing. Those columns which do not have an effect on firing or are not there are not shown. For example, in that table there isn't a column which represents the derivation. The derivation actually represents the deflection of the trajectory because of the rotation of the projectile. So if there is no such rotation, there is no deflection because of the rotation, so this information is not contained in the tables. So there's no need to burden the firing tables with columns that are not relevant or that are empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday we were discussing ellipses, and you mentioned in the innermost ellipse where there was the highest density of shell dispersion, if you take the full ellipse, 50 per cent of the shell dispersion would be in that innermost ellipse. You then said if you cut it in half, you take a half of the -- a semi-ellipse, that's 25 per cent. And then you indicated that a quadrant would be 6.25 per cent. Did you mean that a quadrant would be -- should that quadrant have been 12.5 per cent, which would be half of the 25 per cent, or is the 6.5 correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So it's 12.5 as opposed to 6.25.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yesterday -- do you want to check one of the tables or --

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Yesterday we discussed the suitability of the Old Town for mortars, artillery, and other weaponry. The turrets, there were three or four turrets around the Old Town, kind of at the corners. Are the turrets suitable for firing mortars?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Realistically speaking, that would be very difficult for a number of reasons. The first one would be because the surface is of stone. I don't know how stable that is. Maybe somebody else would know that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. That's one reason. Which means that there would be a large recoil of -- during firing on such a surface, so the mortar would be unstable during firing. Second, if such a mortar was placed on the walls, it would probably be visible from the observation posts in the Zarkovica sector. So such a target -- or such a mortar would be subject to a direct hit. In principle, mortars, because of their construction characteristics, are not placed at the top of a building. They are usually placed in covered firing positions in order to make them a small target which is difficult to find and hit. Placing a mortar on such a building would mean that you are sentencing yourself for destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would the same apply to anti-aircraft weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if we're talking about the -- about cannon, the anti-aircraft cannon are not such a small weapon, so it would not be easy to place it on the wall. The same applies to that as to the mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you discussed the -- the sources of information you used to determine or -- to determine the weapons used by the JNA on the 6th of December in 1991. Based on your experience spending many years in the JNA, in 1991, what type of weaponry would a motorised or infantry battalion possess?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: An infantry motorised battalion would have 120-millimetre mortars, 82-millimetre mortars, anti-tank rockets, mostly the 911 Maljutka type, and recoilless guns, and the rest of the light type of infantry weapons; rifles, machine-guns, sub-machine-guns, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have two questions relating to a map which is marked as Exhibit P160. Sir, on page 12 of your report, you refer to the effective range of a Maljutka being between 500 and 3.000 metres. What is the distance between Zarkovica and the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 2.500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, there are four anti-aircraft positions also listed on that map, one just below the word "Solitudo."

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: One below the word "Lapad," well to the left. One just north of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And one just east of the Old Town, at Ploce. What is the probability, when firing from these locations toward the JNA positions at Srdj, Zarkovica, and Bosanka that anti-aircraft projectiles would land in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the units deployed in Zarkovica and Bosanka were to receive fire from all of those four positions, the trajectories of those weapons would not go above the Old Town. So there is no possibility of it acting -- or hitting the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about Srdj or Bosanka?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness turn the other microphone on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Equal, because if we look at Bosanka and Srdj, they are even further away from that trajectory. They are even further away from town. Srdj is to the north of the Old Town, so there is no possibility. The gun is not facing the town at all. It's facing away from the town if it was directing its fire at Srdj. This also applies to Bosanka. It applies to these two positions, and it applies to Zarkovica as well. To the left, east of the town, those two guns, the trajectories would not pass over the Dubrovnik Old Town. They would go to the north of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And as we're speaking of anti-aircraft weapons, not the heat-seeking rockets or missiles, because we know those can't be used against ground troops or ground positions, the bullets or projectiles fired by the -- fired by the anti-aircraft guns, what calibre are they?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones that are mentioned, or that are seen on the map, are projectiles of 20-millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you show us the size of those with your hand or fingers.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we take the calibre, it's 20 millimetres, so that's 2 centimetres. And this is approximately its size, from about 25 to 30 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I'd like to introduce the diagram that he showed us from his book yesterday. I think he referred to it as a snopar in B/C/S. It's that circular device. One at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you wanting to do something with it or are you wanting simply --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. I'm waiting to get a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is P183.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Next we would like to tender the expert report of this witness, with the footnotes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The expert report is P184.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, we're receiving separately what is apparently the addendum and then a considerable size of paper which is said to be footnotes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that what you're tendering?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: One is the report with the footnotes. The addendum would be a separate exhibit. The report and the footnotes should be one, and the addendum should be a separate exhibit, as with the two supplements that were handed out yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So the footnotes are part of Exhibit P184.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As is the addendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Then the addendum. That's the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you want that as a separate exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Whatever would be easier for the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will treat them all as one exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Including the two supplements, too, supplement 1 and supplement 2 which was offered yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. And finally, there's one other piece of this puzzle, and that's the corrections to the report -- to the report that was filed through the registry a few days ago. Madam Usher, if you could. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That, too, will be part of the one exhibit, Exhibit P184. I'm reminded that we received yesterday two of them as separate exhibit numbers. We seem to be getting very messy, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I didn't offer them yesterday. I just used them to assist with the witness. I don't believe I gave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: All right. Everything, if we can add it all together, is Exhibit P184: Report, addenda, corrections, supplements, footnotes, and the colouring-in pages as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine. Sorry for the confusion, Your Honour. There's several documents. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There were diagrams yesterday, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We offered the diagrams that were used. There was one that was offered. All right. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There was a table of it yesterday, but there were sketches made, diagrams drawn by the witness in his evidence which do not appear to have come into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: One was in fact offered. Why don't we offer the other three as one exhibit, if we could. We'll make the copies at the break, if necessary. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Will you sort out with the court officer during the break exactly what diagrams you tender. Make sure Defence counsel know, and they will all have the number of the diagram that is presently an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll make the copies, too, so everyone will have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And then make your peace with the court officer. Now, while we're in a flurry of exhibits, I've been waiting to hear something about the untendered exhibits concerning the fitness of the accused to stand trial. We haven't yet received the reports from either party. You foreshadowed they would be tendered. We left it, because of the hour, to be done when we resumed. It was not done, and the reports of neither party are presently exhibited, and the Chamber wants to work on them and use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, at this point we would offer the report of the Prosecution's psychiatrists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it that you tender of reports of Doctors Blum, Folnegovic-Smalc, and Matthews as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, which also includes the resumes of each of the doctors, as well as that of Dr. Pressman, the neuro-radiologist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The reports by the psychiatrists for the OTP will be P185.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Weiner, there arrived on my desk a filing containing an affidavit of a Dr. Pressman, of an Elli Remmelezwaan, and of yourself --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- related to the MRI scan. Are you wanting those to be exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's simply a chain of custody affidavit of the MRI scan being taken of the defendant -- or the accused and being passed from the hospital to the Detention Unit nurse to the OLAD unit to myself to Dr. Pressman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will each be received, three separate exhibit numbers. Firstly Dr. Pressman.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P186.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Then Elli Remmelezwaan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And then P. L. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as I know, that concludes all your outstanding exhibits, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll sit down then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But Mr. Petrovic, there is the report of Dr. Lecic-Tosevski and the further report of the 12th of February. Do you want to tender those?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we wish to tender both reports. Unfortunately, in the current situation, due to formal reasons, it is impossible for me to do that because we have not received a sufficient number of copies. They will be ready today. Therefore, I propose and it would probably be appropriate that they be given Defence evidence numbers in order not -- for us not to go back to this issue and waste any more time. However, during the break, we are going to make enough number of copies and distribute it to this Honourable Chamber and to our colleagues from the Prosecution and the Registry. So there are two documents, one dated the 2nd of February and the other one dated the 12th of February, and I propose that both of these documents be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will receive them in anticipation, if you understand that, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The report --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The report on the 2nd of February is marked D83, and the report for the 12th of February is marked D84.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Having tidied up the record, we now return to the cross-examination of Colonel Poje. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. First, I would like to ask the usher if she can see the lectern here in the courtroom, because I can't see it anywhere. I would appreciate if I can have it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreters would like Mr. Petrovic to put the microphone on it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I hope we shall find it in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Poje. My name is Vladimir Petrovic. I'm a Defence counsel, and behalf of Defence, I'm going to ask you questions regarding the report and the addendums to the report and in connection what you have said in this Chamber. First of all, let me just dwell briefly on the data contained in your resume. Could you please tell me, is it true that -- but before that, can you please close the documents that are before you, and if necessary, we are going to consult them if there's no other way to deal with what you are testifying about. Is it true that between 1971 and 1975 you were a battery commander, 120-millimetres UBM52?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that between 1975 and 1978 you were a commander of an anti-tank T-12 gun battery?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that from 1978 you were not a member of the troop but, rather, you worked at the artillery school centre in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1978, I was transferred from Ptuj to the artillery school centre in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In this period after 1978 and until 1991, were you a commander of any artillery unit; a battery, a division, or anyone?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was in -- at the academy the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you left the JNA in 1991. Can you tell us exactly when that happened?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Before the 1st of August, 1991, were you with your unit in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 1st of August, 1991, I submitted an application to be released from the unit, and my application was resolved on the same date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The then Colonel Perisic, Momcilo Perisic. He was the chief of the artillery school centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In that period prior to the 1st of August, was the artillery school centre and the units stationed at the Zadar garrison, were they involved in any combat operation?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I left for the centre, that is before the 1st of August, 1991, the units that were stationed in Zadar and in the school centre were not involved in any combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was your artillery school centre and other units of the Zadar garrison, were they under a blockade imposed by members of the Croatian paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the artillery school centre was concerned, it wasn't under any particular blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were other units in Zadar, JNA units in Zadar, were under blockade?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the school centre and the anti-aircraft system was concerned, the aircraft academy was there, so therefore I wouldn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You don't know what the situation was at the anti-aircraft base in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Zadar. Was water and electricity shut off from your centre?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the time that I was there, we did not have the -- either electricity or water shut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you physically present at your unit before the 1st of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the unit in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you physically with your unit prior to the 1st of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was with my unit -- with my unit at the artillery school centre, teaching the rules of firing, and that all was before the 1st of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you living in Zadar at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was your family there with you?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that families of military officers were exposed at the time by maltreatment and harassment of all forms?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My family was not exposed to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were other families subject to harassment, attacks?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know from the conversations that I had with my colleagues, that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any incidents of setting flats and houses on fire, infliction of serious injuries, murders against members of the JNA and their families in the period before the 1st of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. I don't know of any such incident as far as the institution where I worked was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the Zadar garrison, including the school centre that we are talking about, were there any injuries of soldiers or deaths of soldiers in the period before the 1st of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that. I don't think that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Any officers or junior officers?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you in the war in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, because I left the JNA on the 1st of August, 1991, and the war in Slovenia was already over by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where were you during the war in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Zadar at the artillery school centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: While in Slovenia, the Slovenian paramilitary formations were fighting the JNA, you were a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Slovenian paramilitary formations killed dozens of JNA soldiers at that time that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw it, Your Honour, although it is relevant and we will see why it is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you went from Zadar on the 1st of August, did you join the Slovenian armed forces straight away?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left Zadar on the 4th of August, and I reported to the Ministry of Defence, and I started working.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: From the 4th of August onwards, did you actively take part in the conflict between the units of the Slovenian army and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I worked in the first administration, that is the research, development, and education administration, so I worked on the training of future officers. I was in a special department within that first administration which dealt with the elaboration of programmes for the training of future officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Slovenian paramilitary formations in the period from the 4th of August, 1991, until the end of 1991 - and you joined these formations on the 4th of August - throughout this period were they in an armed conflict with the units of the JNA on their territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The question "paramilitary formations"; there is no evidence of paramilitary formations. There's a Slovenian army. An area declared independence. There's a Slovenian army. And in this Tribunal, "paramilitary formations" usually has a certain meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you be precise in your question, Mr. Petrovic, and we'll see what the witness says of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the position of the Defence is that they were paramilitary formations. Paramilitary formations for the reason that Slovenia had not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, we're not interested in submissions by you or Mr. Weiner about the merits. The point is the form of the question you put to the witness. His answer could be yes or no. What his answer is may turn on whether he agrees that it was a paramilitary organisation that he joined or whether it was an army. You won't know which it means, so you need to pay attention to that. There is a difference between you, I suspect, as to what is the correct description.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try to deal with this in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The armed formations of the Republic of Slovenia from the 4th of August until the end of 1991, were they in a conflict with the units of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were not. I never took part in any military activity from that time onwards.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, I'm not asking whether you took part in this. I'm asking whether the armed forces that you belonged to were in conflict with the units of the Yugoslav People's Army. That is my question.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why are you avoiding a direct answer to the Honourable Trial Chamber to the effect that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object. The witness was asked a question; he's answered the question. He's abusing the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you want something further than "Yes," please proceed, Mr. Petrovic, but the answer that we understand is "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's the only thing that matters to me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: For how long did the armed formations of the Republic of Slovenia, and on how big a territory after the 4th of August, 1991, were in a conflict with the units of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the last JNA units left the territory of the Republic of Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: JNA units on the territory of the Republic of Slovenia, were they exposed to a constant blockade and attacks by the armed forces that you belonged to from the 4th of August, 1991, onwards?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you live in the Republic of Slovenia at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In which town do you live, Mr. Poje?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The barracks of the JNA in Ljubljana, were they under a blockade? Without water, without electricity, constantly exposed to attacks of the forces that you belonged to at that time, Mr. Poje?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not pass by these barracks. I was not in these barracks or around these barracks, so I cannot say. And I cannot say whether they were under a blockade, whether electricity and water had been cut off and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So as a member of the armed formations of the Republic of Slovenia from the 4th of August onwards, Mr. Poje, you do not know anything about Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the conflict between the armed forces you belonged to with the units of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said what my area of activity was in the first administration, and that is the subject matter I dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, at that time did you read the newspapers? Did you watch television? Did you, as a lieutenant colonel in the armed forces of Slovenia, did you have any contact with your colleagues who were engaged in combat operations against JNA units in that period on the territory of the Republic of Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read newspapers. I watched television. I was not in contact with anyone who was actively participating in any activity against the Yugoslav People's Army, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you as a lieutenant colonel in the armed formations of the Republic of Slovenia during the four most dramatic months for the Republic of Slovenia and the former SFRY, you do not know anything about what was going on with the armed formations of Slovenia, what was going on with the Yugoslav People's Army that was on the territory of the Republic of Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know as much as I read and as much as I saw on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was it that you read and what was it that you saw on television, if you as a lieutenant colonel of the armed forces do not have any other information about what was going on in the armed conflict between the forces that you belonged to and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, what was shown in the newspapers and on television was the situation that was then prevalent in the Republic of Slovenia, and that had to do with some conflicts, although as far as I know, at that time there was a cease-fire, and as far as I know, at that time there weren't any combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So when were the conflicts and where? You do know about the conflicts. Where were they and when?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, all the main conflicts ended in the month of July 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the conflicts after the time when you switched sides and when you transferred from the JNA to the Slovenian forces.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many members of the JNA were killed in the territory of Slovenia from the 4th of August, 1991, onwards?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many members of the Slovenian forces were wounded or killed in that period?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What about your colleagues? Were any of them wounded? Were some perhaps killed in the conflict with the JNA at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were they perhaps hiding some information from you because you were in the JNA until the 1st of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is a conjectural question, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your report, why do you say -- I withdraw it. Did you ever take part in any armed operations during your career in the JNA units and after that in the forces of the Republic of Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never took part in any combat operations both when I was in the JNA and later when I joined the Slovenian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why do you say on page 4 of your report in B/C/S, in the one but last paragraph, the one but last paragraph, why do you say: "In war, my --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down. The interpreters do not have the exact reference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the military formation that existed. That was the 3rd M52, 120-millimetre battery in Ajdovscina. That battery was in war, in a possible war within the 3rd Infantry Battalion, the Mixed Artillery Battalion. Never established a regimental artillery group. There were three batteries that we had. One was 76-millimetre B1 mortars, and everybody went to their own battalion. I was the third battery of this Mixed Artillery Battalion, and practically I was within the 3rd Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you to explain the one but last paragraph, the second sentence: "In wartime, my battery supported this infantry battalion in battle." In which war?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I tried to explain that according to the actual establishment, I belonged to the 3rd Battalion, although the battery was in peacetime within the Mixed Artillery Battalion. But in war time, this battery of mine would have supported the 3rd Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you still in active service in the armed forces of the Republic of Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see from your CV, you teach certain subjects. You are assistant director of the second administration, and also you are a counsellor for educational work in doctrine and development for the development of artillery; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment, I am a counsellor of the head of military schools for educational matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: From 1971 until 1989, you were promoted six times in that period from a lieutenant -- from a 2nd lieutenant all the way up to lieutenant colonel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, your last rank in the JNA in 1989 was that of lieutenant colonel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How come that for all of 15 years you were not promoted from the rank of lieutenant colonel further on while during 18 years you were promoted so many times in the Yugoslav People's Army? Why is the reason? Why did you never receive a promotion in the armed forces of the Republic of Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Slovenian army is a small army. That means that it does not have a large number of high ranks. For about five years, or four and a half years, I've been occupying the post of colonel, and of course this is a very small army and it is only natural that you cannot have a large number of very high-ranking positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how did the investigators of the International Criminal Tribunal find you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection. How can he respond to that; how was he selected, by whom --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who contacted you in relation to the elaboration of this expert paper for the International Criminal Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did they contact you? Did they get in touch with you directly? How did that proceed? Could you please describe it.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My former commander of the anti-tank regiment from Ptuj, Stankovic once asked me if I wanted to cooperate with The Hague Tribunal in the area which I actually covered as a teacher. So the commander of the regiment remembered that I had left the regiment and had gone to Zadar to -- as a trainer, so he remembered me. Last year I went -- I had a meeting with Mr. Wiley, and when he found out about my qualifications as a teacher, he proposed that if I wanted to, to cooperate as an expert regarding the control and direction of artillery fire, I could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask your -- did you inform your superior about that?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because I'm still an active military officer, and I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. had to inform my superior officer about that, and I had to obtain permission to cooperate by the government of the Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you speak with anyone else in the period when you were preparing for this testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you speak with anybody from your unit or somebody from the Defence Ministry or Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case, I did not talk with anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you exclusively had contacts with the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got in touch with them when they requested information from me, and I provided that information to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you did not contact anyone with regard to anything that was discussed here today and yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, other than informing them where I am and what am I doing, but I did not actually discuss the case with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know General Milovan Zorc?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to meet with him?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was with him, if I'm not mistaken, in January.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you meet with him before you compiled the report that we are discussing here today?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw General Zorc only on television. He was an advisor to President Kucan. And the first time that I saw him in my life was in January when I came here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You saw him in The Hague for the first time in person?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I saw him in person was in Ljubljana prior to the departure of our aeroplane, if you want to be specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you and General Zorc take part in the conversations with the representatives of the OTP in The Hague together?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you speak with General Zorc about the topic of yours and his testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I might have mentioned which area I was covering. This is a highly specialised topic, and we're speaking about controlling and directing firing, and this is something that he's not interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On page 4 of your report, you say that you fired between 3.500 and 4.000 different shells from a 120-millimetre mortar. What type of mortar?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: 120-millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What model of mortar?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want to be specific, I fired from a UB M52, M75 and M74 mortars of 120-millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Until when were these UBM mortars part of the weaponry of the JNA units?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that until 1990 -- by 1990, the UBM52 was withdrawn from use?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were not used for a while, but I don't know the exact year when they were withdrawn from use.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How is it possible that you don't know up until what period a certain weapon is used by establishment in JNA units, and you are, as you say, training the cadets and future reserve officers in this topic?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I teach the artillery rules of firing. So it's not important which weapons you use, whether this was a 150-millimetre Howitzer or the different types of mortars. These -- what I am teaching are rules of firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Which are applied to specific weapons.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The correction rules for 105 Howitzer or 120-millimetre mortar are more or less the same except for those parts which have to do with establishing the elements of firing, but the rules themselves are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you are telling us that you actually don't know when which weapon was introduced, when it was no longer a part of the establishment. You don't know that, and you're not interested in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection. Objection. That's a misquotation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think your question, if it was a question, Mr. Petrovic, is well beyond the witness's evidence. He has told you that he doesn't know precisely when one type of mortar was withdrawn from active service in the JNA. I don't think it's gone beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know which weapons were introduced into the JNA units?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of other means?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And how do you conduct your training?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is he referring to mortars? Are you referring to Howitzers? These questions are meaningless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is an imprecision, Mr. Petrovic, and in my mind, it's not clear to me whether you're asking before August 1991 or January. So you might take note of Mr. Weiner's concern and mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, do you know, for the period up until August 1991 when a certain type of mortar weapon was introduced or when it was withdrawn from use as an establishment weapon for a JNA unit?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the period before August 1991, do you know when which type of mortar or artillery weapon was introduced or was no longer used by the JNA units?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the formation or the establishment of the JNA units by -- up until August 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know it generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you only know some aspects of the establishment of the JNA units?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know the main or the basic units, elements comprising the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But you don't know the establishment details of JNA units for the period up until August 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know the details. I can tell you the establishment of the units of which I was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the period after August 1991, do you know which weapons were used in JNA units in the period after August until the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which period again?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the period from when you left the JNA until the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which ones. Probably the same ones that were used until August.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the period after August 1991 until the end of 1991, do you know which kinds of ammunition were used in JNA units?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically. Probably those ones which are recorded in the firing tables, and the firing tables have not been changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something very briefly about the UB 52 mortar? Is it true that that mortar, because of its technical characteristics, can be used from any surface, including asphalt, stone?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UB M52 120-millimetre mortar has a recoilless system which alleviates that problem and could in principle be used on hard surfaces as well, even though, practically, I never used it on such a surface because -- nor did I hear of anyone using the mortar on such a surface. It's always dug in, in principle. The base is always dug in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that that mortar could be used in populated places, with a -- on a hard surface also?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that as this mortar was being withdrawn from the JNA forces it was being transferred to the TO units as a weapon for their use?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear something about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the TO units were armed with the 120-millimetre UB M52 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mortars, although I did not ever see myself such a territorial unit -- Territorial Defence unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know which services or branch or arm of service are in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Infantry, armoured units, mechanised units, artillery, engineering, anti-biological, nuclear and chemical defence, communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are these separate services of the army which have their own rules, rules for each arm and service?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Each arm and service has its own combat rules to use during combat for the units of that arms or service.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are the combat rules for artillery the main rules for the artillery arms and services?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is the rules for -- rule for battalions the main rules for -- used by the infantry?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's for the use of an infantry battalion. There is a special combat rule for the use of the regiment and the brigade and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The rules, are they used to provide in a unified way for the implementation of combat operations of the units of the arms and services, artillery rules for the artillery, and then the brigade and battalion rules for the infantry?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the artillery combat rules are the main rules used by the artillery units during combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As part of the artillery arms and services.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The rules for the battalion, the infantry, mechanised, mountain, and armoured is the rules for a battalion, an infantry battalion or a mechanised battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is the use of a battalion regulated by these rules and defined whereby a battalion is defined as a basic tactical unit of the infantry?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you kindly look at page 5 of your report. The title in B/C/S is -- this is paragraph 8. The title is -- of this segment of your report is "Technical aspects of artillery," and in parentheses "(mortars)." Could you tell us, why did you formulate the title or the heading of this section of your report in this way, "Technical aspects of artillery (mortars)"? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a certain period, the 120-millimetre mortars were an artillery weapon. Lately, the 120-millimetre mortars are an infantry weapon. This is so in the JNA. And that is why, in order to avoid any errors, when I say "artillery," I included the mortars also because I didn't want it to seem as if I excluded the mortars. That is why they are mentioned separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So a mortar is an infantry weapon, a 120-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now a mortar, as far as our system is concerned, is an infantry weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is a mortar -- was a mortar in 1990 and 1991 also an infantry weapon, a 120-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at that time mortars were not part of infantry weapons even though the artillery training centre organised training in the infantry in the Sarajevo school centre to control and direct mortar fire. In the 1990s and maybe a year or so before that, it was -- there was talk that mortars would be transferred to the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that from 1985 the JNA units was -- had by establishment 120-millimetre mortars exclusively of the infantry units?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to 1991, the artillery school centre trained officers and reserve officers to control and direct fire for mortar units, and in 1991, I used, I fired from 120-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Since you fired from those mortars, this is -- but this is not something that is relevant to us here right now. What I'm asking you is whether you know that as of 1990 -- 1985, a 120-millimetre mortar was a formation weapon of the infantry units.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we please go on a break now, if you think that this is the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We will break for the first morning break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, since you just told us that at the relevant period the 120-millimetre mortar was an infantry weapon as per establishment, could you please tell us why on page 5 of your report - that's question number 8, item A - referring to firing support, why in interpreting what the fire support means of infantry weapons, why are you citing the combat rule of the -- of another arm of the armed services, and that is of artillery?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this section of the report which deals with fire support, I described artillery support provided by mortars. Although mortars were infantry weapons, nevertheless they were subjected to artillery rules in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you claim that in 1991, the use of mortars was regulated by artillery rules? Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The combat rule for artillery refers both to artillery as it was at the time, including mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I must ask you again. Are you saying that in 1991, the use of infantry weapons, and that is 82- and 120-millimetre mortars, were the subject of artillery combat rules?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 120-millimetre mortars were subject to the rules -- combat rules for artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How is it possible that combat rules for artillery refer to artillery weapons? Where and when have you heard of that? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even though mortars were infantry weapons, their calibre and their mode of their use were used according to artillery rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that, for example, if a Maljutka 9K11 rocket is an anti-tank guided missile, does that mean that this rocket is subject to the rules of rocket units?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How, then, was it possible for infantry weapons to be subject to the rules of artillery? I'm talking about 120-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed, and I still believe, that 120-millimetres were governed by firing rules for artillery and rules of engagement for artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the 1991 rule -- combat rule for artillery, there is no mention of mortars as artillery weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rule that you are mentioning I haven't seen before, and I didn't apply it in compiling my report concerning the year 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I have no doubts that you did use it, but if I tell you that in 1991 rule of artillery combat, there is not a single mention of mortar as artillery weapon, does that mean that your report is incomplete?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think he should present it to him and let him see it if he's going to ask him a question about it. If he's going to continue to question him about a specific rule, he should present it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That would be the normal procedure, as you know, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Chamber will be presented with this, and I now will move on to my next question. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why in this question 8 under item (a), why are you talking about fire support? Why are you compiling inadmissably two different rules of two different arms of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I made this report, I used this rule of artillery, and I believe that a 120-millimetre mortar unit should be governed by artillery rule -- combat rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If you please take a look on page 5 of the B/C/S report. That's 8(a). The first four paragraphs under this item, you rewrote verbatim from the 1982 artillery rule; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On the same page, or under the same item, the remaining seven paragraphs you rewrote verbatim from the battalion rules which apply to infantry; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why did you do that? Why did you in the first place rewrite things?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this first part, I wanted to explain what fire support was - in fact, artillery and mortar support - and that is why I describe what general support was, what direct support was, and later in this paragraph I explained how a battalion fire group was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why did you not write anywhere in the report that these first two -- four paragraphs were rewritten from the artillery combat rule and that the remaining seven paragraphs you had rewritten from the battalion combat rule? I'm referring to pages 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I don't want to apologise or excuse myself for that, it's probably an omission on my part while I was preparing the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How is it possible to use a unit of a specific arm under two combat rules for two different arms? How is that possible? Have you ever come across that in your practice?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to be a commander of a 120-millimetre unit in the -- mortar unit in the mixed division, and that means that practically we were part of the 3rd Infantry Battalion, and my battalion, in its name, had connotations that it was an artillery unit, and I was part of the 3rd Infantry Battalion. There is nothing disputable about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, there is a lot that is disputable. What you're talking about took place in 1970, 1971, 1975, or 1978, and that applies to those years, but you just told us that from 1985, mortars were infantry weapons as per establishment. Therefore, my question is: After 1985, how was it possible for one type of weapon used by an infantry or a mechanised unit to be governed by rules of two different arms, which you are implying in your report on pages 5 and 6? We are talking about the period between 1985 and 1991. How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that fire support, whether by artillery weapons or mortars 120-millimetres, was one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us why this paragraph that refers to battalion support, fire support group, and that is the first paragraph that deals with infantry battalions, why did you not quote it exactly? Why did you modify this rule referring to a battalion?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I don't know how the rule reads exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let me read it for you. That's page 17, item 19, battalion rule. A battalion fire group -- do you have this rule in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If he's going to read a rule -- if he's going to confront the witness with a rule, he should show it to him, especially if it's a long rule or several sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is the position, Mr. Petrovic, but you may be saved because the witness appears to have access to it himself. He's just taken it from his box -- his bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The rule is very short, it just has one sentence. I don't know if we have the same edition. In any case, item 19 of the battalion rules --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please read slowly, Mr. Petrovic, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to you, Your Honour, and to our interpreters. Thank you, Your Honour. There are so many things to be done today, and we are really in a hurry. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Have you found it, Mr. Poje?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does it read exactly what it reads in your report?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a phrase missing in the last sentence quoting artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The last sentence reads: "It is set up by organic and attached weapons and mortars." Is that what the last sentence in your report reads?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does it read as I read it?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why did you add here "and 120-millimetre mortars"? Why did you add this phrase, and why did you omit the words "artillery weapons and mortars" where there's an apparent and obvious distinction between artillery weapons and mortars? Why did you quote this erroneously?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no reason for me to omit this, because I thought that organic and attached weapons include artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You left this out because you persistently tried to depict a mortar as an artillery weapon, and for that reason, you omitted this very clear distinction quoted in Rule 19, where there is a distinction between artillery weapons and mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Form of the question. It's argumentative, and it's misquoting the witness's statement too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It can be easily rephrased, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think this is very clear, and I won't dwell on this issue any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Poje, in the last paragraph on page 5, is it true what you say here, that a battalion commander has sole authority over commanding the battalion and all units attached to it for execution of a combat task?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 6 now. Paragraph 1 on page 6 of the B/C/S version reads: "The battalion fire support group captures in an assault firing positions one to two kilometres before company front line and provides firing preparation and support." Is that how it reads?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, when you looked at the map that my learned colleague showed you yesterday where the JNA unit positions were plotted on the 6th of December, you noticed there that the fire support group number 3 of the 3rd Battalion was at least 5.000 metres behind the front line of the battalion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Less than 5 kilometres, about 4 kilometres, and that is what I said in my report, because the battalion was on the defensive and that probably the fire support group was deep into the rear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: From that you arrived at a conclusion that the 3rd Battalion, among other indicators, on the 6th of December was on a defensive.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The map we saw yesterday was dated the 2nd of December, and what I said in my report is correct, and that means that a 3rd Battalion was on defensive. And for that reason, 120-millimetre mortars and the fire support group were relatively withdrawn into the rear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct to say, since you have in front of you the battalion rule, and if you look at rule 321, and that is the rule pertaining to battalion on defence, and that is explaining combat disposition -- do you see this rule 321?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It reads that: "A battalion on defensive is deployed in-depth Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. amounting to one to two kilometres on a mountainous terrain and on a mountainous terrain at around five kilometres."

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The width of defence of a battalion on a mountainous terrain can be between two and five kilometres. And as you say, on a mountainous terrain, up to five kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So I interpreted this correctly?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In other words, in a situation that you saw on the map on the 2nd of December, the battalion fire group was very much deep into the defence area of a battalion at its rear borderline?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said in my report they were on the defence and that the 3rd Battalion group was very, very deep into the perimeter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The usual depth of defence of a battalion is two to three kilometres, and here we have a battalion fire group positioned between four and five kilometres in depth. If a battalion was planning an attack, the first operation would be to pull forward -- Your Honour, just one moment. There's an answer missing to my question asked about -- that's on page 41, line 9. The witness said "Yes." Maybe I can read it in order to make it more clear and to clarify this, because his answer is missing. Therefore, Mr. Poje, the usual depth of defence of a battalion is two to three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And here on the 2nd of December, the battalion fire group was positioned between four and five kilometres from the front line.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That means deep into the rear.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Next question: If a battalion moves from the defensive to the offensive, if it plans to attack, the battalion fire group gets closer to the front end of the battalion, as it says in the rules on attack. It gets one to two kilometres closer in relation to the front end; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the battalion were preparing to attack, it would have to bring it closer, the battalion fire support group, closer to its front end. It would have to be positioned about one or two kilometres away from the front end of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, we are going to move on to the next question. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Poje, on page 6 of the B/C/S version of your report, the second paragraph which says: "Fire preparations for an attack in the battalion mean coordinated action of the artillery (mortars and infantry units)." Is it correct that this wording is not contained in the battalion rules?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it has to do with fire support in attack. So practically that is what it is, fire support in attack. Any unit; a battalion, a company, anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please look at rule 213, 213 in the battalion rules. Have you found it, Mr. Poje?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the second paragraph on page 6 of the B/C/S version, you copied out the first paragraph of rule 213; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, if you look at battalion rule under 213, where does it say there "organised and coordinated fire in response to artillery," then "(mortars)"? Where does that say? And you told us yourself that you copied it out.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say I copied it out. Secondly, this refers to mortars as well. In this entire report, I'm talking about the efficiency of mortar fire, first and foremost, and that's why I accentuated that, that it pertains to mortars as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So artillery is one thing and mortars are another thing.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can put it that way if you wish. I'm sorry. At any rate, a 120-millimetre mortar is not the same thing as a rifle, so that is why I attached more importance to mortars as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You attached importance to mortars because you were asked to describe the operation of mortars, and the only thing that is in dispute is why you are marking mortars -- or, rather, classifying mortars as an artillery weapon when it is not one. And that's what you told us yourself about half an hour ago.

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with what you said just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So it's quite unnecessary, is it? Quite unnecessary. It is quite unnecessary for you. When you quote rule 213 in your report, you include something which was never part of the rule. Artillery is one thing, and a mortar as an infantry weapon is a completely different thing altogether. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although I still think there is no problem when mortars are included as well. So if we say that it's an infantry weapon according to its specific way of operation, it is. If you exclude mortars, again I don't think much has changed because they will always remain infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please look at this same page. We're just going a bit lower. We're now looking at subparagraph (b).

utterances.speaker: JOZEF POJE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You say that the artillery is a combat arm of the army that has great firepower. What does that have to do with what we are discussing, with mortars?
